items.stem: A customer sends a dish back because it is too salty. Which way of deciding who should change their work matches backpropagation?

options.text: Start at the complaint and work backward, asking how much each person's work affected the result.
options.feedback: Backpropagation passes blame backward from the loss, layer by layer, using what each step handed to the next.

options.text: Ask each person to change their work at random and see whether the complaint goes away.
options.feedback: That is closer to nudging each weight and running the whole network again, which is the costly approach backpropagation avoids.

options.text: Blame only the last person who handled the dish, because that person served it.
options.feedback: That ignores the earlier steps, and the earlier weights are exactly the ones that need a slope.

options.text: Ask everyone to change their work by the same amount and see what happens.
options.feedback: Each weight affects the result by a different amount, so each needs its own slope.

items.stem: A network has two inputs, two hidden units and one output. Two of its six weights connect to the output. How do the other four get their slopes?

options.text: From the blame passed back by the units closer to the output.
options.feedback: The blame at the output is passed back through the hidden units, so each earlier weight gets its slope from numbers already worked out.

options.text: By nudging each one and running the whole network again.
options.feedback: That is the costly method that backpropagation avoids, because it needs a full run for every weight.

options.text: They need no slopes, because only the last layer is adjusted.
options.feedback: Every weight in the network is adjusted, so the four earlier weights need slopes too.

options.text: Directly from the loss, the same way the output weights do.
options.feedback: Only the output weights sit close enough to the loss for that. The other four affect the answer through the hidden units.

items.stem: A team needs slopes for a network with 2 billion weights. Method A nudges each weight and runs the network again to see whether the loss improved. Method B uses backpropagation. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A needs about 2 billion full runs for one step. B needs about one forward and one backward pass.
options.feedback: Backpropagation reuses numbers already worked out, so it gets every slope for about the cost of one forward pass.

options.text: Both methods need about the same amount of computing, because both find the same slopes.
options.feedback: They differ by a factor of billions for a network this size.

options.text: Method A is cheaper, because it avoids the backward pass that Method B needs.
options.feedback: Avoiding the backward pass means repeating the whole forward pass for every weight.

options.text: Method B needs 2 billion passes, but each pass is cheaper than a full run.
options.feedback: Method B needs one backward pass in total.
